Stock rules are handed to the domain service StockManager, not written inline.
mapToDto() turns the domain Order into the application OrderDto, which is an application-layer task.
No persistence, HTTP or framework calls appear in src/application/usecases/PlaceOrderUseCase.ts.
Borderline: the checks for an empty line list and quantity <= 0 in execute() run on the request DTO. They could arguably live on the Order entity, but they count as input validation here.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: PlaceOrderUseCase does the job of an application-layer use case. It checks the incoming CreateOrderRequest, fetches products through the domain ProductRepository interface, builds the domain Order, hands the stock check and reservation to the domain StockManager, saves through the OrderRepository interface and maps the result to an application DTO (OrderDto). The file has no persistence code (SQL, ORM, file I/O), no transport or framework code (HTTP, request/response objects) and no presentation logic. Checking that each product exists needs a repository lookup, so it belongs in the use case. Generating an order ID and mapping to the DTO are normal application tasks. The borderline point is the two checks in execute(): an order needs at least one line, and quantity must be greater than zero. These could be read as invariants the Order entity should enforce. Because they run on the request DTO before the Order is built, I treated them as input validation, which is acceptable in the application layer, and did not count them as a clear misplaced responsibility.
